title: Learning to Judge Fairly
readingBrief: Cyrus tells his mother Mandane how he judged a dispute involving two boys and two coats. His attention to which coat fits each boy leads to a correction about ownership and rightful possession. Begin with the learner deciding what question a judge must answer. Keep the conversation within Xenophon’s literary portrait of Cyrus; it is not independent documentation of Persian classroom practice.
grammarObjectives: Introduce the subjunctive as a mood, with its characteristic vowel patterns and present/aorist formation in the assigned regular verbs.
Distinguish present and aorist aspect without treating the subjunctive as an ordinary future tense.
Teach the chapter’s principal uses through deliberation, exhortation, prohibition, and purpose as assigned; distinguish questions about what to do from factual questions.
Identify the clause signal, verb form, subject, and intended meaning. Defer systematic general-clause work to Lesson 39 and the full conditional system to Lesson 44.
application: Use independently composed questions and proposals around the dispute: what should the judge examine, and for what purpose should he ask? The teaching sentences are adaptations, not quotations. Virtue focus: usefulness, fairness, and ownership may point in different directions.
cultureBrief: Who owns the better-fitting coat? A two-stage decision activity first asks students to allocate the coats, then reveals the ownership question. Introduce the difference between an ethical story and historical evidence about Persian institutions. Mandane is an active questioner; explain that her voice reaches us through a male Greek author.
workIntroduction: Cyropaedia overview; distinguish Cyrus the Great from Cyrus the Younger and explain the work’s educational purpose.
assessmentBrief: Parse and interpret subjunctives, rewrite a factual sentence as a deliberative question, and defend a judgment using evidence from the passage. Score the reasoning, not agreement with a preferred answer.
readingBannerBrief: A young Cyrus listens while two boys hold different-sized coats; Mandane anchors the conversation.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate Persian textile and clothing scene, with garments and weaving tools; no duplicate of the judgment scene.

title: Justice in the Household
readingBrief: Ischomachus describes selecting and training a housekeeper and using rewards and punishments to encourage trustworthy conduct. Read the household through the responsibilities of the wife and the enslaved housekeeper as well as those of the owner. Ask who defines good conduct and who can challenge that definition. Keep the housekeeper’s unrecorded thoughts and dialogue explicitly outside the source account.
grammarObjectives: Form and recognize subjunctives of the assigned -μι verbs, including δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι, and ἵημι as covered by the chapter.
Connect each form with its principal parts and distinguish present from aorist stems.
Extend Chapter 21 uses with controlled purpose, exhortation, and deliberation practice.
Contrast finite subjunctives with familiar imperatives and infinitives; retain agreement and accent practice.
application: Compose short proposals about giving rewards, placing objects in someone’s care, and establishing an orderly household. Make the speaker and the intended beneficiary explicit. Virtue focus: accountability must include the person who exercises power.
cultureBrief: The household as a workplace. Students inspect a labeled inventory and consider who keeps records, performs labor, and receives credit. Explain enslaved status directly and distinguish delegated responsibility from freedom. Compare a rule protecting property with a rule protecting the person who handles it.
workIntroduction: Oeconomicus overview; revisit household order from Module III through justice and unequal authority.
assessmentBrief: Choose and produce appropriate -μι subjunctives, explain the purpose of a proposed rule, and identify one limitation of the owner’s perspective.
readingBannerBrief: Ischomachus’ wife and a housekeeper consult an inventory in a courtyard; show skilled work and purposeful action.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate storeroom with measured containers, textiles, and an inventory tablet; do not reuse the people-centered Reading composition.

title: The Accusation
readingBrief: After the retreat, soldiers accuse Xenophon of striking men. He questions an accuser and defends his own actions. Use a short exchange rather than the whole speech. Preserve the difference between an allegation, Xenophon’s response, and the army’s reaction. The narrator is also the accused leader, so the account invites scrutiny rather than an automatic verdict in his favor.
grammarObjectives: Clauses of fearing, including μή and μή οὐ, with mood and sequence handled at the chapter’s level.
Indefinite and general clauses: recognize relative or temporal signals, ἄν where appropriate, and the force of the subjunctive.
Introduce the chapter’s indirect statements and indirect questions; preserve the original speaker, pronouns, and question word.
Compare a direct claim, a reported claim, and a fear. Gloss any secondary-sequence optatives retained in an original extract until Lesson 43.
application: Use fear of injury or disorder and reports of the disputed conduct to make clause relationships meaningful. Keep the accusation distinct from a statement accepted as fact. Virtue focus: leaders remain answerable for their treatment of others.
cultureBrief: An army holds its leaders to account. Students sort evidence cards into accusation, response, corroboration, and missing information. Discuss physical coercion and the limits of hearing a subordinate’s complaint through the commander’s own narrative.
workIntroduction: Anabasis overview; explain how the return journey continues after the famous sight of the sea.
assessmentBrief: Translate a fear clause without reversing its meaning, classify general clauses, and convert a short question into an indirect question using taught constructions.
readingBannerBrief: An accuser addresses Xenophon before assembled soldiers, with enough space to show the hearing rather than a fight.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate camp assembly layout showing listeners, officers, and the speaker’s position.

title: Speaking the Truth
readingBrief: The Athenian victory at Arginusae is followed by accusations over the failure to rescue men. Select competing reports and the dispute over trying the generals collectively. Include Socrates’ refusal to support unlawful procedure as Xenophon reports it. Provide a short factual bridge to the outcome; the lesson must not imply that his objection prevented the executions.
grammarObjectives: Indirect statement with infinitive, supplementary participle, and ὅτι or ὡς: governing verbs, subject case, and relative tense/aspect.
φημί: assigned forms, enclitic behavior where relevant, and its use in reporting.
Articular infinitive: article, case, expressed subject, and common functions.
Relative-pronoun antecedents and the assigned special cases, including attraction where covered.
Prepositional prefixes and euphony: explain the chapter’s spelling changes and connect compounds to their dictionary forms.
application: Recast short statements from the debate in appropriate reporting constructions. Do not treat infinitive, participle, and ὅτι as mechanically interchangeable after every verb. Virtue focus: truthful evidence and lawful procedure both matter.
cultureBrief: Victory, grief, and a hurried decision. Use a sequence diagram distinguishing council, assembly, and law court. Students identify the procedural safeguard at issue and explain why an angry majority still needs evidence. The culture activity concerns this extraordinary proceeding, not a claim that every Athenian trial worked this way.
workIntroduction: Hellenica overview; explain how an historian arranges speeches, decisions, and consequences.
assessmentBrief: Follow speaker and subject through three reporting constructions; analyze an articular infinitive; resolve a relative antecedent; explain one compound form. Finish with a brief evidence-based account of Socrates’ objection.
readingBannerBrief: A tense assembly with Socrates among the presiding officials; avoid modern courtroom furniture or gavels.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate view of the Pnyx and a labeled civic-process illustration, clearly marked as reconstruction.

title: A Ruler and the Common Good
readingBrief: Simonides proposes that a ruler gain honor by helping the community prosper. Select a few proposals about public benefit, rewards, and shared success. Ask whether benevolent management is enough to make power just. Treat the exchange between Simonides and Hiero as a literary dialogue, not a transcript or proof that the historical ruler adopted the proposals.
grammarObjectives: Further regular and irregular comparison: stems and the assigned comparative and superlative forms.
Declension of comparatives and recognition of alternative forms where assigned.
Comparative constructions and distinctions among comparative, superlative, and contextual intensive meanings.
Object clauses after verbs of care or effort using ὅπως with future indicative; distinguish these from purpose clauses using a subjunctive.
application: Compare private wealth with public benefit and express care that a civic task will be completed. Virtue focus: assess a ruler by effects on the community and by the limits of accountability.
cultureBrief: Who benefits from a prize? Students allocate a fictional civic budget among festivals, agriculture, and public amenities, then state who gains and who is missing from the discussion. The budget is a course exercise, not a reconstruction of ancient accounts.
workIntroduction: Full first introduction to Hiero, including speakers, structure, tyranny, and the unresolved question of reform.
assessmentBrief: Decline selected comparatives, interpret the standard of comparison, and contrast ὅπως + future indicative with an earlier purpose construction.
readingBannerBrief: Simonides and Hiero converse in a restrained Sicilian palace setting, with civic activity beyond.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate public festival or agricultural-prize scene emphasizing the community rather than the ruler.

title: What is Justice?
readingBrief: Hippias challenges Socrates to explain justice. Their discussion connects just conduct with law and then considers unwritten laws. Select the objection that laws change and Socrates’ response. Return explicitly to the procedural dispute in Lesson 40: learners should examine how an appeal to law differs from compliance with whatever a powerful person demands.
grammarObjectives: Optative formation in the assigned regular verbs; recognize characteristic endings and connect stems to familiar tense/aspect systems.
Optative expressing wishes, with the relevant particles.
Potential optative with ἄν; distinguish a possibility from an assertion or a wish.
Optative in subordinate clauses at the chapter’s level; introduce sequence without treating every past reporting verb as requiring mechanical replacement.
application: Add labeled course sentences wishing for fair decisions and considering what a just citizen might do. Use these to practice the mood without claiming that the chosen ancient lines contain every target form. Virtue focus: turn a definition into a standard that can be tested.
cultureBrief: Written law and unwritten obligation. Students compare a civic rule, a shared custom, and a claim of divine authority. Keep the universality of the unwritten laws as a claim made in the dialogue, not an established fact about every society.
workIntroduction: Memorabilia overview; explain the collection’s defense of Socrates and the purpose of its ethical conversations.
assessmentBrief: Distinguish wish, potentiality, and assertion; form optatives; explain Hippias’ objection fairly before evaluating Socrates’ answer.
readingBannerBrief: Socrates and Hippias discuss justice with a small listening group.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate close view of a reconstructed inscribed law and a civic oath setting; no fabricated readable ancient inscription.

title: Law and Fear
readingBrief: Critias removes Theramenes from the protected list of Three Thousand and has him seized despite his appeal at the altar. Focus on the manipulation of procedure and the fear of those watching. Theramenes was himself an oligarch with a complicated political record; the lesson need not make him innocent of every earlier action to examine the injustice of this proceeding.
grammarObjectives: Optatives of the assigned -μι verbs, with present and aorist stems and distinctions in formation.
Optative in indirect statements after historical reporting verbs; explain retention of original mood where appropriate.
Indirect questions in secondary sequence: question words, speaker reference, and mood choices.
Recover a plausible direct utterance from a report without assuming that every reported version has only one possible original.
application: Report commands, objections, and questions in a past narrative. Separate the narrator’s account from Critias’ legal claim. Virtue focus: fear can empty a legal institution of its protective function.
cultureBrief: An altar and a list of names. Explain the Thirty, the restricted citizen list, and the council setting. Ask which safeguards are removed at each stage. Use a sober account of seizure and death; no graphic illustration is needed.
workIntroduction: Hellenica return panel; connect this episode to the work’s treatment of political power and civic conflict.
assessmentBrief: Parse -μι optatives, explain indirect questions in historical sequence, and identify where a procedural claim masks coercion.
readingBannerBrief: Theramenes appeals at the council altar while officials and guards stand apart; show the danger without violence.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate reconstruction of the council chamber and a writing tablet representing the citizen list.

title: If They Act Justly
readingBrief: Read the settlement after civil conflict, the return to civic life, and the agreement not to recall past wrongs, with the exceptions named in the source. Explain that reconciliation is a political achievement with terms and limits. Do not equate it with forgetting every injury or treating all parties as equally responsible.
grammarObjectives: Conditional sentences: build the assigned system, including open conditions, future more vivid and less vivid, general conditions, and contrary-to-fact conditions.
Identify protasis and apodosis, tense/mood, negation, and ἄν; interpret the speaker’s stance before naming the category.
Adverbial accusative and accusative of respect.
Accusative absolute, especially impersonal expressions; compare it with the genitive absolute.
Verbal adjectives in -τέος: personal and impersonal constructions as assigned, necessity, and the relevant agent construction.
application: Use clearly invented civic proposals to explore what follows if people keep or break an agreement. Practice necessity with concrete obligations. Virtue focus: reconciliation requires enforceable commitments as well as restraint.
cultureBrief: How can former enemies share a city? Learners design a short settlement with provisions for safety, accountability, and return. Compare it with the source’s actual terms. Avoid turning this exercise into a modern legal judgment or an undifferentiated celebration of amnesty.
workIntroduction: Hellenica return panel; revisit the distance between ending a battle and restoring civic trust.
assessmentBrief: A two-part assessment separates the conditional system from accusative constructions and -τέος. Students then explain how changing a condition changes a proposal’s meaning.
readingBannerBrief: Citizens return to Athens after the settlement, with cautiously welcoming groups rather than universal celebration.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate oath-taking and civic-reassembly scene, framed as a historical reconstruction.

title: The Defense of Socrates
readingBrief: Hermogenes asks why Socrates has not prepared the expected defense. Socrates presents his conduct throughout life as his preparation. This begins a four-lesson sequence rather than repeating the whole trial immediately. Explain Xenophon’s stated reliance on Hermogenes and distinguish this work from Plato’s Apology.
grammarObjectives: Perfect and pluperfect middle/passive forms: formation and meanings, including the chapter’s finite and nonfinite forms.
Perfect middle/passive participles: declension, agreement, and substantival or circumstantial use.
Perfective/resultant-state aspect and the pluperfect’s past reference point; compare these with the aorist.
Reduplication, augment, vowel-initial patterns, and consonant-stem changes.
Dative of agent and its limits; distinguish it from other familiar dative functions.
application: Use adapted descriptions of what has been done, what stands recorded, and what had already been decided. Keep active perfects glossed until Lesson 46. Virtue focus: assess the relationship between a person’s conduct and persuasive self-presentation.
cultureBrief: Preparing to speak for oneself. Explain the role of a defendant’s speech and why Xenophon concentrates on Socrates’ manner. A practice activity compares an appeal based on conduct with an appeal to pity; it must not suggest that all persuasion is dishonest.
workIntroduction: Full introduction to Xenophon’s Apology and its relationship to Memorabilia and Plato’s different account.
assessmentBrief: Identify reduplication and stems, parse a perfect participle, explain a resultant state, and distinguish an agent dative from possession or means.
readingBannerBrief: Hermogenes speaks with Socrates before the trial in a quiet Athenian setting.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate display of speech preparation and court materials, with period-specific objects checked before illustration.

title: Why They Are Angry
readingBrief: Read the audience’s reaction to Socrates’ claims and Xenophon’s explanation of his manner. Add a brief, explicitly separate comparison with the association of Critias and Alcibiades with Socrates in Memorabilia. These connections provide context for hostility; they are not a substitute indictment, and they do not establish every juror’s motive.
grammarObjectives: Perfect and pluperfect active formation, including -κα and -α patterns and the assigned principal parts.
Reduplication, stem changes, common irregular forms, and the temporal relation of the pluperfect.
Active perfect aspect and its contrast with aorist narration and present states.
οἶδα and its assigned forms: perfect morphology with present meaning; distinguish knowing from having seen in translation.
application: Use statements about what speakers know, have done, or had previously heard. Separate knowledge from reported reputation. Virtue focus: a judgment about a person needs evidence stronger than association or resentment.
cultureBrief: Reputation in a small political community. Students sort claims into formal charge, remembered association, narrator’s explanation, and conjecture. Present the recent civic trauma without teaching that it makes the verdict inevitable.
workIntroduction: Apology return panel with a Memorabilia comparison; both works defend Socrates, but their structures and immediate purposes differ.
assessmentBrief: Distinguish perfect active from aorist and perfect middle/passive, interpret οἶδα correctly, and revise a claim that overstates what the source establishes.
readingBannerBrief: Listeners react differently as Socrates speaks; avoid depicting a uniformly irrational mob.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate timeline of 406, 404–403, and 399 BCE with civic landmarks rather than another courtroom image.

title: The Trial of Socrates
readingBrief: Assemble a manageable courtroom reading: the charges, Socrates’ answers, reactions, verdict, and his response. Use short bridges for omitted material. Keep Xenophon’s version internally consistent and identify it throughout; do not silently insert famous passages or penalty proposals from Plato.
grammarObjectives: Complex indirect statement in primary sequence: organize the constructions already learned into sustained reporting.
Track relative time and aspect in infinitives and participles; distinguish these from finite ὅτι/ὡς clauses.
Resolve nested subjects, pronouns, negatives, and subordinate clauses while preserving the force of the original claim.
Practice reporting verbs in present or future contexts without mechanically changing the whole passage’s tense.
application: Give an adapted present-tense reporting frame around selected claims: the writer explains, Socrates says, or the accuser maintains. Label this frame as course adaptation. Virtue focus: fair reporting requires representing another person’s argument accurately before judging it.
cultureBrief: How to read an ancient trial account. Build a diagram separating prosecution, defense, verdict, and penalty. Introduce civic juries and the differences between ancient procedure and a modern courtroom; use verified evidence for any objects or numerical details added in the full lesson.
workIntroduction: Apology return panel; compare a literary defense with a verbatim transcript and explain what the text can and cannot establish.
assessmentBrief: Produce a short report in primary sequence, annotate two levels of speaker reference, and explain one point on which the accuser’s claim differs from the narrator’s judgment.
readingBannerBrief: Socrates addresses citizen jurors in a historically cautious courtroom reconstruction.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate view of voting equipment and a water clock, based on verified museum references at image-authoring time.

title: Justice and the Soul
readingBrief: End with Xenophon’s retrospective assessment of Socrates and a short return to civic reconciliation. The final question is whether a good life and a just city can be judged by the same evidence. “Soul” here concerns character and ethical life; the reading does not present Xenophon as supplying the immortality arguments of Plato’s Phaedo.
grammarObjectives: Complex indirect statement in secondary sequence: historical reporting verbs, optative substitution where appropriate, and permissible retention of the original mood.
Preserve relative time and aspect in infinitives and participles; distinguish those constructions from finite-clause sequence.
Resolve nested clauses, pronoun reference, negation, and the author’s distance from a reported claim.

Cumulative integration of subjunctive, optative, conditions, articular infinitives, advanced accusatives, verbal adjectives, and perfect/pluperfect systems. New Chapter 30 instruction precedes the cumulative assessment.
application: Recast a small portion of Lesson 47’s report in a historical frame and explain each necessary change. Then compare a claim about Socrates’ character with a claim about restored civic trust. Virtue focus: careful judgment includes admitting what the evidence does not settle.
cultureBrief: How a life becomes a remembered example. Students compare Xenophon’s praise with the actual episodes studied. A final gallery revisits the coat dispute, household labor, the soldiers’ hearing, civic reconciliation, and Socrates. Each item identifies its work and source status.
workIntroduction: Memorabilia return panel and a course-wide guide to Xenophon’s genres; learners should be able to locate a work and explain why it was written.
assessmentBrief: Complete a supported unseen adaptation, a primary-to-secondary reporting task, focused grammar questions, and a short source-based reflection comparing two works. Allow reasoned disagreement with Xenophon; assess accurate reading, grammatical explanation, and use of evidence.
readingBannerBrief: A reflective teaching scene recalling Socrates with listeners from different ages, labeled as course reconstruction.
cultureBannerBrief: A separate closing panorama of the city and its civic spaces, connecting individual conduct with shared life.
